Before looking at the specific meanings, notice that lush almost always signals the same underlying idea: generous, rich abundance that delights the senses. Whether you're describing a rainforest or a piece of music, "lush" tells the reader that something is not just present, but overflowing with richness. Keep that feeling in mind — it connects every meaning of the word.
Meaning 1 — Thick, Abundant, and Healthy Plant Growth (The Most Common Meaning)

This is the heart of the word. When you call a plant, a garden, a field, or a forest lush, you mean it is growing vigorously, densely, and healthily — and that it looks wonderfully green and full.

It's not just some growth. Lush growth is rich growth — the kind of green that comes from plentiful rain, good soil, and plenty of sun. Picture a tropical rainforest: tall, thick trees, enormous leaves overlapping each other, soft moss covering every rock, vines hanging in every direction. That is the perfect image of lush. Or picture a meadow after a rainy spring — the grass so thick and deeply green it almost doesn't look real. That, too, is lush.

The word naturally paints a picture of abundance that feels generous, almost overwhelming in the best possible way.

Examples:

  • "The valley was covered in lush green fields."
  • "Lush tropical vegetation surrounded the waterfall."
  • "After weeks of rain, the garden became beautifully lush."
Meaning 2 — Luxuriously Rich (For Objects, Places, and Experiences)

"Lush" naturally expanded from nature into the wider world to describe anything that feels luxuriously rich, generous, and indulgent — not just plants. Here, the word suggests the kind of high quality that you notice immediately, the kind that makes you slow down and appreciate what's in front of you.

A lush hotel suite has thick carpets, heavy curtains, and furnishings that feel expensive and deeply comfortable. Lush velvet has a deep, rich look and feel. A lush landscape painting in a film makes every scene feel like a feast for the eyes.

Think of this meaning as the plant imagery transferred to the human world. Just as lush vegetation is generous and full, lush surroundings or objects are generous and full in quality, beauty, and richness.

Examples:

  • "The palace was decorated with lush, gold-detailed furniture."
  • "She wore a dress made of lush, dark velvet."
  • "The film had a lush visual style — every frame was a painting."
Meaning 3 — Rich and Full to the Senses (Music, Food, Color, and More)

Closely related to Meaning 2, "lush" is widely used to describe a sensory experience — something you hear, taste, see, or feel — that is unusually full, warm, and deeply satisfying.

In music, a lush sound is one that feels rich, layered, and warm — like a full orchestra playing together with beautiful harmony, filling the room completely. Thin, spare, or minimalistic music is the opposite of lush. In food, a lush flavor or texture is one that feels generous and rich on the palate — think of a deeply creamy chocolate mousse or a wine with many complex, full flavors. In art or film, lush colors are deeply saturated, warm, and visually beautiful, not dull or washed out.

This is an especially expressive use of the word and very common in reviews, creative writing, and descriptions of art.

Examples:

  • "The orchestra produced a lush, sweeping sound that filled the hall."
  • "The chocolate cake had a lush, velvety texture."
  • "The painting glowed with lush, golden tones."
Meaning 4 — British & Australian Informal: Attractive or Wonderful

In informal British and Australian speech — especially in Wales and parts of England — "lush" is used as a casual, enthusiastic compliment meaning attractive, gorgeous, or simply wonderful/great. It works for people, things, and experiences.

A British teenager might say "That song is absolutely lush!" meaning "That song is amazing!" or "He's lush!" meaning "He's really attractive!" It carries the warmth of the other meanings — the idea of something being richly, pleasurably good — but applied as everyday slang.

Important note: This meaning is regional and informal. You would not use it in formal writing, and American English speakers do not generally use "lush" this way. If you're in the UK or Australia in a casual conversation, you may very well hear it, but be aware it sounds natural only in those informal settings.

Examples:

  • "That new café on the high street is lush."
  • "Did you see her dress? She looked absolutely lush."

Occasionally, mostly in older or informal speech, "lush" is used as an adjective to mean drunk (intoxicated by alcohol). For example: "After four glasses of wine, he was feeling quite lush." This connects loosely to the idea of being "saturated" — just as lush vegetation is saturated with water and richness, a person who is lush is saturated with alcohol.

As a noun in this same informal register, a lush refers to a heavy or habitual drinker, and carries a somewhat negative or judgmental tone. Both uses are fairly dated today and not especially common in mainstream modern speech, so while it's useful to recognize them, you are unlikely to need to use them yourself.
The Connotations: How Does the Word Feel?

"Lush" is almost always a compliment or a positive description. It carries warmth, richness, and pleasure in all of its main meanings. When someone calls something lush, they are signaling that it is abundantly, generously good — not in a restrained way, but in a full, overflowing way.

It is a somewhat sensory and evocative word — it doesn't just describe facts, it paints a feeling. Saying a forest is "dense" is factual; saying it is lush makes the reader almost feel the greenness and richness of it. This is why "lush" is popular in poetry, creative writing, film descriptions, food writing, and travel writing, anywhere the goal is to make someone feel something rather than just understand it.

SituationWhat "lush" means

When describing nature and plants, lush means thick, green, and abundantly healthy. When describing objects, places, or decor, it means richly luxurious and beautifully high-quality. When describing sensory experiences like music, food, or color, it means deeply rich, full, and satisfying. In British/Australian informal speech, it means attractive or wonderful. And in older or informal use, it can mean drunk.

The golden thread connecting all of these? Richness and generous abundance — something overflowing with quality, fullness, and pleasure.
